opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the key realization for me was that the most valuable thing a supervisor provides isn't hours of hands-on help. It's judgment. Doing research well involves an enormous number of small decisions: which direction to pursue, when to abandon an idea, which experiment will actually tell you something, when a result is too good to be true. Early-career researchers often lack the intuitions to make those calls well, and a few minutes from someone who has made many of those mistakes can save them weeks.

So I try to structure things to get the most out of that judgment. I have short, frequent check-ins rather than long meetings. Scholars come in with a summary of what they've done, what they're confused about, and what they plan to do next. Most of my value comes from saying things like, "That's a rabbit hole, don't bother," or, "That result is surprising, sanity-check it before building on it," or, "You're overcomplicating this. Try the dumbest possible baseline first." Those interventions are cheap for me and very high leverage for them.

I also lean heavily on scholars working in pairs or small groups and helping each other. A lot of the day-to-day unblocking, like debugging code or talking through an idea, doesn't need me. Peers can do that, and they learn a lot from teaching each other.

And a big part of it is just being explicit about research taste. I try to explain why I'm making a recommendation, not just what it is, so that over time they internalize the heuristics and need me less. The goal is that by the end of the program they're asking the questions I would have asked before I get the chance.

It's not a perfect substitute for intensive mentorship, but I've been pleasantly surprised by how far a few well-spent hours a week can go, especially when the scholars are talented and self-directed, which MATS scholars generally are.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a supervisor can offer valuable research judgment in a few minutes, while early-career researchers often lack the intuitions to make those decisions well themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, because on the face of it, a few hours a week per scholar sounds kind of pathetic, right? Like, how can you possibly add that much value? And I think the key insight is that research is really, really high variance, and most of the variance comes from a small number of decisions.

The way I think about it is that a research project has a bunch of different phases. There's the phase where you're choosing what to work on, there's the phase where you're figuring out how to approach it, there's the phase where you're actually doing the experiments, there's the phase where you're interpreting the results, and then writing it up. And the amount of time each of those takes is very uneven. The actual doing of the experiments is where most of the hours go. But the decisions about what problem to work on, what approach to take, when to pivot, when something is a dead end versus when it's a promising thing you should push harder on — those are things that take maybe a few minutes of actual decision-making, but they have enormous consequences for the entire project.

And those are exactly the places where experience matters the most. If you've been doing interpretability research for several years, you've developed a bunch of intuitions about what kinds of things tend to work, what kinds of things tend to be dead ends, what the existing literature already says about something so you don't reinvent the wheel, which results are actually surprising versus which ones are kind of trivially explained by some boring thing you haven't thought of. And a lot of the ways that early-stage researchers waste time is by not having those intuitions yet. They'll spend three weeks going down a path that I could have told them in five minutes was probably not going to work, or they'll get a result and be really excited about it, and I'll be like, "Hmm, have you checked whether this is just an artifact of how you're tokenising things?" And it turns out it was.

So if I can intervene at the right points, I think a few hours a week can genuinely change the trajectory of a project by a lot. I'm not there to do the work. I'm there to be a kind of error-correction mechanism and a prioritisation mechanism.

The other thing I'd say is that I try to be really deliberate about how I use the time. So I'll have a weekly meeting with each scholar, and I want that to be very high density. I'll ask them to send me a written update beforehand so I'm not spending the first fifteen minutes just getting up to speed. And then the meeting itself is mostly me asking a lot of questions. What have you found? What do you think it means? What are the other possible explanations? What are you planning to do next, and why that rather than this other thing? And often just the act of being asked those questions is really valuable, because it forces people to articulate things they'd been kind of vaguely feeling but hadn't really examined.

And then outside of the meetings, I try to be available asynchronously. If someone's stuck on something, or they've just gotten a surprising result and they're not sure what to make of it, they can message me and I'll often respond pretty quickly. That doesn't take much of my time but it can unblock someone who would otherwise lose a day.

I think there's also a bigger-picture thing, which is that a lot of what I'm trying to do isn't actually about this specific project. It's about trying to teach people how to do research. Because the goal of MATS isn't really to produce one paper. It's to produce researchers. So when I'm pushing back on someone's reasoning or asking them why they're prioritising something, part of what I'm hoping is that they internalise that way of thinking and start asking themselves those questions. And if that happens, then the value of my few hours a week compounds over their entire career, which is a pretty good return on investment.

Now, I do want to be honest that there are real costs to this model. There are things I can't do. I can't pair-program with someone for an afternoon. I can't notice the subtle things you notice when you're sitting next to someone and see them getting frustrated. There's a lot of tacit knowledge that's hard to transmit in a one-hour meeting. So I don't think a few hours a week is as good as being a full-time mentor. But I think it's a lot more than a few hours' worth of value, and given the constraints — there just aren't that many experienced interpretability researchers, and we all have day jobs — I think it's a pretty good trade-off. It lets me supervise more people than I otherwise could, and I think the marginal value of getting one more person into the field doing good work is really high.

r001.rationale: The response says key research decisions can take only minutes yet have enormous consequences, and explains that experienced researchers’ intuitions help scholars avoid dead ends and catch errors they may not recognize themselves.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing is that the value of supervision isn’t necessarily proportional to the amount of time you spend on it. A lot of the value is in helping someone choose a good problem, and then noticing when they’re going down a path that probably isn’t going to work.

Someone can spend a week implementing an experiment, but the question of whether that experiment will actually distinguish between two hypotheses might be something we can make progress on in a half-hour conversation. I can ask: what are you trying to learn? What would change your mind? If you got the result you’re hoping for, would that actually support your explanation, or could something much simpler be going on?

And I think there’s a lot of tacit knowledge in research. Which results are surprising, which approaches are worth trying, when to keep pushing and when to move on. You don’t need to be there for every line of code to help someone develop that judgment.

There are limits, obviously. This works much better if the scholars can make progress independently, and have other people to talk to when they get stuck. But if my few hours help them spend the rest of their week on a more useful question, that can be a pretty substantial contribution.

r001.rationale: The response says a brief conversation can improve problem choice and experimental reasoning, and describes research judgment as tacit. It does not clearly communicate that these judgments would be difficult for MATS scholars to replicate on their own.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that the value of supervision isn’t necessarily proportional to the amount of time you spend on it. Someone can spend a week pursuing a direction that isn’t going to work, and a half-hour conversation can sometimes save them that week. Or they’ve got an interesting result, but they haven’t quite noticed what’s interesting about it, and you can help them see the next experiment to run.

So I try to focus on the things where my judgement is most useful: choosing a tractable question, figuring out what would actually constitute evidence, and noticing when a project needs to change direction. The scholars do almost all of the actual work. My contribution is helping that work point somewhere useful.

There’s also a teaching component. I don’t just want to say, ‘Do this experiment.’ I want to explain why I think it’s the right experiment, so that over time they get better at making those decisions themselves. Ideally, the amount of supervision they need goes down as the programme goes on.

r001.rationale: The response says a half-hour conversation can save a week spent on an unworkable direction, and describes helping scholars recognize what is interesting and choose useful next steps. It also says scholars need to build these decision-making skills over time, communicating the difference between the supervisor’s quick research judgment and the scholars’ initially limited ability to make it themselves.
